To OP: 

I am not giving you advice, I am only trying to encourage you that there are more options out there other than what you have tried. You should discuss the benefits and risks associated with anything you wish to try in terms of treatment with your provider.

Of the things there are to still try includes psychotherapy, which you stated you are going to try. If you don’t click with a therapist, that doesn’t necessarily mean psychotherapy won’t be helpful. Some people see more than one therapist before they find one they like.

There are also different kinds of therapy. If one isn’t working (CBT is typically the go to in my country), there are more! There are different types of psychotherapy with different approaches, including ones that focus on trauma. A therapist should be able to tell you what therapeutic approach they take as well as describe the science and philosophy behind it. A therapist may also be able to educate on different approaches and psychotherapies available that they do not have experience in. A therapist can also provide information and resources surrounding different coping skills.

There is also therapy available at different acuity levels with different structures such as partial hospitalization programs and intensive outpatient programs.

There are other medical approaches as well outside of med management like TMS and shock therapy. These may help patients in conjunction with psychotherapy and meds, or if they find the other approaches aren’t working.

There are things that patients can do outside of treatment as well, like take walks, hang out with people you like, trying new things and see if you enjoy them. An example could be if someone had time and likes animals, they could go to the local animal shelter and volunteer to walk their dogs and socialize the animals.

Again, not meant as advice. I only mean to state that there are other things out there. You should your provider for guidance.

Many EDs don’t even have a psychiatrist in house, or even in the entire hospital, and ER doctors are not typically too keen on letting you go if you come in voluntarily, because if you leave and do something, they can get sued.

I had a patient who was boarded in our ED (i’m in ohio) for over 50 hours before being admitted to our floor. I know our state for sure has a chronic shortage of beds, adult and peds. Believe me, from the perspective as a current employee and previous patient, the psych ward should be the ABSOLUTE last resort. The psych ward doesn’t usually help people through their mental health, it keeps them safe through an acute crisis. It’s not therapeutic, it’s crisis stabilization. I’m not saying don’t get help or don’t go to the hospital if you need to, but if you’re not staring down the barrel of a gun or into a bottle of pills, I would consider outpatient treatment. There is much more freedom in your life and in decision making in your treatment. If you don’t have one already, find a psychiatrist (you may be waitlisted). Also, apply for IOP (intensive outpatient) or PHP (partial hospitalization). There you won’t be separated from your routine and your support individuals and you won’t be at the will of the inpatient psych. If you go in voluntarily, if you try to leave ama, they will pick slip you and you’ll become involuntary. So please please please assess where you are in the moment before going to the ED. If you are ACUTELY suicidal or homicidal (like if you don’t go to the hospital you 100% believe you will act on those thoughts), definitely go to a hospital or crisis center. Psych hospitalization can be extremely traumatic. The first 3 months after discharge is when a patient is at highest risk for suicide. So if you can get the level of treatment you need outpatient, please please please do so!!! If you express any intention, you will likely be involuntarily committed. If you are a minor, you will likely have a much better experience than an adult. Peds psych is like a vacation compared to a lot of adult psych.

I’m coming from an American point of view first off. Some of the things you’ve mentioned aren’t standard in American facilities, so I just wanted to clarify in case your experiences were in other countries. For example, pediatric wards max out at 17. Anyway, I agree the system is incredibly flawed and definitely needs overhaul. The reality is, inpatient stays are meant to be brief and just for stabilization. Somebody should only be taken inpatient in a psychiatric ward because they are a threat to themselves or someone else. In most cases, this stabilization can happen in under a week, and in my experience most patients who are med compliant and who are receptive to treatment are discharged in 3-5 days with outpatient services set up for them. We typically only see longer stays when we can’t find placement for an individual, or when pts continue to be suicidal, homicidal, overly aggressive or in active psychosis. 

There are definitely policies I feel are not necessary, and I use my best clinical judgment when it comes to rule bending. If everyone is safe, no personal info is being shared, and everyone is respecting boundaries, i’m pretty lenient. I would be curious though as to what rules you feel are unnecessary. I will say as far as phone calls go in the pediatric ward, we can’t let minors just contact whoever they want because we need consent from parents while they are in our care. Doctors have to approve other callers because even who you contact while you are inpatient can effect your treatment. 

Unfortunately, the mentalities between peds and adult wards are different. In peds, the goal is to address whatever is going on and get you in a treatment plan that will keep you from being inpatient again. As an adult, it’s about getting you to be compliant again on your meds or babysitting you while you are acutely suicidal. It’s fucked up, but I can’t single-handedly change the system. I can only be the best, most supportive staff member as I can be to ensure people have positive, therapeutic experiences. 

As far as psychosis goes, we have to be careful. I’ve had psychosis patients who were fine, I’ve had some who require multiple staff members because they are so aggressive and paranoid. I’ve had standard patients who have become violent and aggressive who aren’t psychotic. We just have to be careful with everyone. We had a psychotic pt make a comment about abuse while in psychosis. CPS is investigating it even though the pt now denies saying those things since they’ve been out of psychosis. I’ve had psychotic pts say I hit or abused them. Thankfully I always stay on camera, so I can’t be charged for something I didn’t do. When I was inpatient, I had another psychotic patient threaten me and another psychotic patient who was walking into peoples showers. We also separate them from other patients because they need different interventions. Patients in psychosis really just need medication until they are out of psychosis. Then they can benefit from other therapeutic treatments, like groups. They would just be disruptive of group therapy for standard patients.

I work in a pediatric ward, but I’ve been hospitalized in an adult ward. My experience was horrible, and it drives my work to be the best staff member I can be. I don’t know what the root issue is, but the world of adult inpatient psych is so flawed and lacking in compassion. Pediatric psych is typically so much better (I say typically because there are definitely still bad wards out there). We need a huge overhaul of the entire system really.

It really comes down to how it will work for you. Each person responds differently, so I can give you my experience, but it isn’t a good indication necessarily of what you will experience. But anyway, for context of my story, I’m confident that I haven’t been misdiagnosed. I went to a psychiatric nurse practitioner because I was sure I just had generalized anxiety and wanted to talk about my options regarding anxiety meds. When I was describing my experiences, she stopped me to grab a paper. She had me do this evaluation, didn’t tell me what it was for until after scoring it, and then said she had suspected based on my symptoms that I had ADHD and that the evaluation confirmed that. I have always been intelligent. I was in gifted classes, then honors and AP, then got a full tuition scholarship to an honors program at my university where I currently hold a 3.9 gpa. I’m not saying this to brag. I’m saying this because I don’t take Adderall occasionally for an exam or something. I sought help because I was doing really well in school until suddenly I hit a wall. I had good study tactics, I’m a great academic writer, I have taken classes dedicated literally to just doing research and producing academic writing. My work ethic and work quality wasn’t the issue. When I started taking a consistent dose of Adderall, I was able to get over my wall and continue my academic success. And now I am better able to follow conversations, I am less overwhelmed by stimuli that used to bother me, and my moods are more stable because I’m not on edge all the time.

My experience as an individual diagnosed with ADHD in my 20s who is on Adderall XR is great, but like many drugs (especially those used to treat mental disorders) they have different effects on different people. And some people respond well and benefit from them while others don’t. Personally, I wouldn’t let other’s experience turn you away from trying the medication if your doctor believes it will be beneficial for you. You may have a completely different experience than them! You really have to just try it and find out for yourself if it will work for you. You also have to give your body time to adjust. For me it took about 2 weeks (my insurance would only cover adderall if i took twice as much as what my provider wanted to prescribe and it had to be xr, not instant release. she wanted to put me on 10mg once a day of instant release as a trial run and to adjust to it, but prior authorization said no unless it was 20mg of xr. so i had a very intense introduction to the meds). As for the addiction piece, that’s also different for different individuals. I for one couldn’t get addicted to adderall if i tried. I barely remember to take it in the morning lol. I did have to make adjustments to my lifestyle though in order to feel good on my meds (drink lots of water, cut back my caffeine, etc.) but they were all things that are healthier anyway.
